Repo: /home/lane/MythosMini — a 1,050,241-param byte-level (vocab 257) looped-shared-block transformer trained on fineweb-edu, benchmarked on WikiText-2 byte PPL, BLiMP, ARC-Easy against the Tiny-ML leaderboard (overall = mean of blimp, arc, normalized wiki score; efficiency = overall/log10(params+1) so PARAMETER GROWTH IS PENALIZED only logarithmically — doubling params costs ~5% efficiency but any overall gain counts fully). Current pipeline: procedural Dyck warmup -> 2B-token training (NAdamW, WSD schedule) -> 3-round recursive STM -> benchmark all checkpoints -> SLERP tournament -> SFT instruct phase -> instruct SLERP. Architecture: 4 prelude + 1 shared block looped 2-6x with per-loop LoRA + 4 coda, dim 96, RMSNorm/RoPE/SwiGLU, tied embeddings, DSA-style sparse attention (shared model-level lightning indexer, top-128 keys, 64 local window, FlexAttention short path, chunked long path, 1M max context), FP4 E2M1 QAT on all linears. Recent regression: moving the indexer from per-attention to one shared model-level indexer + detaching the indexer bias for prelude/coda blocks raised throughput 0.85->1.19 Mtok/s but the verification run scored 59.47 overall vs 60.40 before, AND its STM round 3 NaN-diverged (prior runs round 3 gave +0.57; NaN also seen once before with output-embedding centering). All-time best: 60.41 (recursive STM, commit accd37b). GPU: one RTX 5090 32GB, torch 2.10.0+cu128. Known: full-model torch.compile broken (inductor dtype bug + flex recompile issues), STM phase runs at only ~76 ktok/s vs training 1.19 Mtok/s. USER GOAL: push output quality as far as possible toward Gemma-class coherence (text in/text out) — ambition is the point; consider parameter growth, distillation, synthetic data, anything that fits one 5090.

Research via web search: state-of-the-art techniques (2024-2026) for maximizing quality of SUB-10M-parameter language models. Focus on: hyperparameter scaling laws for tiny models (muP, depth/width, lr vs size — note current peak_lr 3e-3 for dim 96), modern optimizers (Muon, AdamW variants, schedule-free), data curriculum beyond simple filtering, repeated-epoch vs fresh-data tradeoffs at 2B tokens for 1M params (extreme overtraining — what do papers say), and embedding/softmax tricks for byte-level models. Each finding must be implementable on one RTX 5090 in this codebase.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about μP (Maximal Update Parametrization) and its application to learning rate scaling for small language models:

## Overview

Maximal Update Parametrization (muP) proposes a learning rate scaling designed to keep the update dynamics of internal representations stable across different model widths. Learning rate optima, momentum, and even per-layer multipliers remain stable under arbitrary width scaling, for both LLMs and vision architectures.

## Application to Small Language Models

The approach involves tuning hyperparameters on a smaller proxy model and directly copying these hyperparameters to the large-scale target model. When migrating training configuration from a small proxy model to larger model sizes, μP has been proposed including width scaling and depth scaling, which facilitate transferring the hyperparameters from smaller models to the training of larger models.

## Recent Developments (2025)

Recent work has extended μP to Mixture-of-Experts LLMs, ensuring constant optimal learning rate with increasing model width and number of experts, with empirical transfer holding unless fine-grained expert scaling is introduced.

## Implementation Tools

PyTorch and Jax/Flax packages automate implementation of μP, notably through the github.com/microsoft/mup package.

However, it's worth noting that the scaling rules of muP rely on strong assumptions about geometric alignment, which may only hold briefly at the start of training in practical setups like LLM training.

## Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) Overview

The Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) is a novel byte-level large language model (LLM) architecture that processes raw bytes instead of tokens.

## Hash N-Gram Embeddings

For each position i in the byte sequence, n-grams are computed for n∈{3,4,…,8} representing consecutive bytes up to 8-grams. Each n-gram is hashed to an index in a fixed-size embedding table using a rolling polynomial hash function. 

Hash n-gram embeddings are very effective with very large improvements in BPB (bits-per-byte), and the most significant parameter is the per-ngram vocab size and smaller ngram sizes are more impactful than larger ones.

## Model Architecture

BLT encodes bytes into dynamically sized patches, which serve as the primary units of computation. Patches are segmented based on the entropy of the next byte, allocating more compute and model capacity where increased data complexity demands it.

Bits Per Byte (BPB) is used to measure uncertainty at the byte level, with lower BPB scores indicating higher efficiency. In compute-optimal scaling studies up to 8B parameters and 4T training bytes, BLT models matched or slightly outperformed BPE Llama 3 models in terms of BPB on the training distribution.

## Core Problem

A specific instability that often occurs at the end of training is output logit divergence.

## Existing Mitigation Strategies

The most widely used mitigation strategies, z-loss and logit soft-capping, merely address the symptoms rather than the underlying cause of the problem.

**Z-loss:** Z-loss is proposed to encourage the softmax normalizer to be close to 0. Z-loss is an effective measure to prevent the logits from diverging, which stabilizes the training process.

**Logit soft-capping:** Logit softcapping (Gemma-style) is the preferred method for attention/LM-head logit stabilization; z-loss and QK-norm are alternatives.

## Alternative Approach

Recent research proposes output embedding centering (OEC) as an alternative. The instability is analyzed from the perspective of the output embeddings' geometry and anisotropic embeddings are identified as its source. Both variants of OEC outperform z-loss in terms of training stability and learning rate sensitivity, ensuring that training converges even for large learning rates when z-loss fails.

## Softmax Bottleneck in Small Language Models

Small language models suffer from saturation, characterized as a drop in performance at some advanced point in training followed by a plateau, which can be explained by a mismatch between the hidden dimension of smaller models and the high rank of the target contextual probability distribution. This mismatch affects the performance of the linear prediction head used in such models through the well-known softmax bottleneck phenomenon.

Models based on less than roughly 1000 hidden dimensions tend to adopt degenerate latent representations in late pretraining, which leads to reduced evaluation performance.

## Mixture of Softmaxes (MoS) Solution

The "Softmax bottleneck" is addressed through the proposed Mixture of Softmaxes (MoS) model, which conceptualizes language modeling as a matrix factorization problem. MoS computes K Softmax distributions and uses a weighted average of them as the next-token probability distribution.

Standard Softmax-based language models with distributed word embeddings do not have enough capacity to model natural language, which is referred to as the Softmax bottleneck. Mixture of Softmaxes is more expressive than Softmax and other surrogates considered in prior work.

## Overview

The Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedule is a learning rate strategy that progressively stabilizes deep network training through warmup, plateau and decay phases. In contrast, cosine annealing with a short linear warm-up is popular largely because it packs several desirable mathematical properties into one simple, two-hyper-parameter curve.

## Key Performance Differences

Empirical and theoretical analyses show that WSD outperforms cosine decay by enhancing scaling law efficiency and optimizing the bias–variance trade-off. More specifically, linear decay to zero outperforms partial decay (e.g., cosine to 10%), offering improved bias reduction and variance suppression; D2Z provides compute savings over standard schedules, especially at high tokens-per-parameter.

## Practical Advantages of WSD

The Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedule uses a constant learning rate to produce a main branch of iterates that can in principle continue indefinitely without a pre-specified compute budget. This is a significant advantage over cosine scheduling, which depends on the total number of steps.

A long flat phase followed by a sharp cooldown often outperforms continuous cosine decay.

## Recommended WSD Parameters

Practical recommendations for WSD scheduling include: Warmup: typically 1–2% of total steps; linear ramp to stabilize gradients · Stable plateau: 60–80% of training; maximal exploration and noise injection · Decay: 10–25% of training; use sqrt or lowered-linear shapes for optimal bias–variance trade-off.

## Theoretical Perspective

Recent theory shows that warmup-stable-decay can match or beat cosine (in certain regimes). However, no schedule dominates universally though. Cosine is good enough on many standard vision tasks, but plateau-ing or refined linear decays are competitive elsewhere.

## The Core Problem

Standard knowledge distillation requires that teacher and student models share an identical tokenizer and vocabulary, since the most common form of distillation operates at the logit level where the student is trained to match the teacher's probability distribution over a fixed set of vocabulary tokens. A logit vector of size 50,000 from the teacher cannot be directly compared to a logit vector of size 32,000 from the student.

## Universal Logit Distillation (ULD)

Boizard et al. (2025) introduced Universal Logit Distillation (ULD) loss based on optimal transport theory, which allows for distillation across different architectures and tokenizers without requiring them to share the same vocabulary. More specifically, ULD trains the student via next-token prediction plus a Wasserstein distance loss between the teacher logits and the student logits at every step.

## Other Approaches

Beyond ULD, researchers have explored alternative methods:

- MinED (Wan et al., 2024) aligns the student and teacher logits by greedily aligning every token in the students' vocabulary with the teacher token which has the minimal Levenshtein edit distance to the student token.

- Multi-Level Optimal Transport (MultiLevelOT) advances optimal transport for universal cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation by aligning the logit distributions of the teacher and student at both token and sequence levels using diverse cost matrices.

# Byte-Level Distillation for Cross-Tokenizer LLM Transfer

## Method Overview

The paper introduces Byte-Level Distillation (BLD), which enables knowledge transfer between models using different tokenizers by operating at a shared byte-level interface. Rather than attempting vocabulary alignment, the approach converts teacher outputs to byte probabilities and adds a lightweight byte-level decoder head to the student model.

## How Byte-Level Learning Works

The student learns through two parallel objectives:

1. **Byte-level supervision**: A lightweight module (10 parallel linear projections) predicts bytes, receiving both cross-entropy and KL-divergence losses from teacher byte probabilities
2. **Token-level supervision**: The original token decoder continues training on standard next-token prediction

The teacher's byte probabilities are computed using an approximation algorithm from prior work that marginalizes over all possible tokenizations. The byte-level head is removed after distillation, leaving a standard token-level model.

## Computational Requirements

**Single GPU feasibility**: Not practical for typical setups. The authors required "approximately 2 days" using "four NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs" just to precompute byte probabilities for the training dataset. Processing involves computing probabilities for 100-150 byte sequences at "approximately 10.4 seconds per sample" with their optimized configuration.

Training itself uses LoRA (rank 64) on frozen backbone weights, making it more efficient than full fine-tuning.

## Results Achieved

Performance is mixed across three tasks:

- **BPE-to-BPE transfer**: Competitive with baselines but inconsistent—leading on PiQA (75.68) and AGI-ZH (35.97) but significantly lagging on instruction-following (IFEval: 30.58 vs competitors' 58-62)
- **BPE-to-byte transfer**: All methods suffer major degradations (~13-21 points). BLD marginally leads on PiQA (67.52) but no clear winner emerges
- **Cross-tokenizer distillation** (8B→2B): BLD achieves best GSM8K (62.55) but trails on MATH (20.08)

**Key finding**: The authors conclude that "no method...achieves consistent improvements across all benchmarks," establishing that cross-tokenizer distillation remains "a largely open problem."

findings.detail: The rigorous 'Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers' benchmark (arXiv 2509.02046) found matrix-preconditioned optimizers (Muon, Soap) give ~1.4x data-efficiency over AdamW at 0.1B params, and the speedup is INVERSELY proportional to scale — at 1M params the gain should be >=1.4x. Muon powers every modded-nanogpt speedrun record (124M GPT-2 in ~3 min) and Kimi K2/GLM-4.5 at trillion scale. Implementation: in /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/training/optimizer.py replace build_nadamw with a two-group optimizer: Muon (Keller Jordan's ~60-line Newton-Schulz orthogonalization, momentum 0.95, lr ~0.02-0.05, runs fine in bf16 on one GPU) for all 2D weights in the shared Block/Attention/SwiGLU/prelude/coda (transformer.py classes at lines 103-300), and AdamW for embed/loop_embed (transformer.py:306,311), RMSNorm gains, LoRA A/B, and the sparse indexer. Note Muon LRs do not follow Adam LR intuitions — keep the existing WSD schedule multiplying both groups. Gradients accumulated across the 2-6 loop iterations of the shared block are just summed grads on one matrix — Muon handles this unchanged.
findings.expected_gain: Literature predicts >=1.4x effective-data multiplier at this scale, i.e., the 2B-token run behaves like ~2.8B tokens. On the leaderboard that plausibly translates to several tenths of overall score; it also compounds with every other change. NAdamW (current) was one of the benchmarked baselines and lost to Muon at every scale tested.
findings.risk: Interaction with FP4 E2M1 QAT in training/fp4.py is untested (Muon orthogonalizes the master-weight gradient, which should be fine since QAT uses STE, but verify on a 100M-token smoke run). Muon LR needs its own short sweep; a wrong value can diverge — gate behind a config flag and compare against an NAdamW control.

findings.title: Peak LR 3e-3 is likely 5-20x too LOW for a 1M-param model; sweep upward with the Step Law as the prior
findings.detail: The Step Law fitted on 3,700 runs (arXiv 2503.04715) gives eta_opt(N,D)=1.79*N^-0.713*D^0.307. Plugging N~1e6 non-embedding params, D=2e9 tokens yields eta~6.7e-2 — 22x the current peak_lr=3e-3 in /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/config.py:80. This is an extrapolation below their fitted range, so don't trust the constant, but the direction is unambiguous: optimal LR rises steeply as N shrinks (muP says 1/width for hidden layers; dim 96 is ~10-80x narrower than models 3e-3-class LRs were tuned for). Also their batch-size law B(D)=0.58*D^0.571 gives ~120k tokens/step optimal at D=2e9 (~232 seqs of 512) — check effective_batch in training/loop.py:135 against this. Action: run 100-200M-token sweeps at peak_lr in {6e-3, 1e-2, 2e-2, 4e-2} (with the stability package below), pick by wiki byte-PPL at matched tokens. Note 'Weight Decay may matter more than muP for LR transfer' (arXiv 2510.19093): LR transfer is mediated by weight decay, so sweep jointly with finding on wd below.
findings.expected_gain: Under-tuned LR is typically the single largest free win in small-model training; literature suggests loss equivalent to 1.5-3x more data if current LR is far off optimum. Cheap to verify with short runs before committing the 2B-token budget.
findings.risk: Higher LR is the classic NaN trigger and this codebase already has a NaN history (STM round 3, output-embedding centering). Must land the stability finding first. Extrapolated formula could overshoot badly — trust the sweep, not the constant.

findings.title: Decay LR to zero (D2Z), not to 10% of peak — gains are largest exactly in this extreme tokens-per-param regime
findings.detail: 'Straight to Zero' (arXiv 2502.15938) shows linear decay-to-zero beats decay-to-10% consistently, with the gap growing at high tokens-per-parameter ratios — this model trains at ~2000 tokens/param vs Chinchilla's 20, the most extreme D2Z-favorable regime in any paper. Change: /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/config.py:81 min_lr_fraction: 0.1 -> 0.0 (floor computed in training/scheduler.py:10). Keep WSD shape (WSD itself is well supported, e.g. arXiv 2410.05192), just take the decay leg to 0. Optionally also try extending decay_fraction from 0.2 to 0.25 — 'sqrt or lowered-linear decay shapes, 10-25% of training' is the recommended WSD recipe. Bonus: D2Z's variance-suppression argument suggests the final checkpoint will be a better SLERP-merge candidate (less noise in weights), which feeds the existing tournament in reslerp.py.
findings.expected_gain: Paper reports consistent final-loss improvements that grow with tokens/param; at 2000 TPP expect a measurable wiki-PPL drop for a one-line change. Essentially free.
findings.risk: Very low. Only caveat: STM and SFT phases that resume from the final checkpoint start from a zero-LR endpoint, which is the standard setup anyway.

findings.title: Stability package: z-loss + final-logit softcap + QK-norm (fixes STM round-3 NaN, enables higher LR)
findings.detail: The observed failures (STM round-3 NaN; NaN with output-embedding centering) match the canonical 'output logit divergence' end-of-training instability. Battle-tested mitigations (arXiv 2410.16682 'Methods of Improving LLM Training Stability', Gemma 2, PaLM): (1) z-loss — in /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/training/loop.py:49-54 compute_loss, add 1e-4 * (torch.logsumexp(logits, -1)**2).mean(); (2) Gemma-style final-logit softcap — in transformer.py:355 replace functional.linear(x, self.embed.weight) tail with 30*torch.tanh(logits/30) (LM head only — do NOT softcap attention scores, it would break the FlexAttention score_mod path at transformer.py:188); (3) QK-norm — RMSNorm on q and k after project_heads (transformer.py:125), the strongest known guard for high-LR training. Note: the existing center_output_embeddings flag (config.py:96) is exactly the OEC method from arXiv 2601.02031, which that paper claims strictly beats z-loss — the previous NaN with it suggests an implementation bug (likely centering must be applied as a mean-subtraction on the tied embedding INSIDE the head computation each step, not as a weight mutation that also perturbs the input embedding since embeddings are tied). Worth re-deriving, but z-loss is the safe default.
findings.expected_gain: Recovers the +0.57 that STM round 3 contributed in healthy runs (the NaN-diverged verification run scored 59.47 vs 60.40); z-loss/QK-norm are prerequisites for the LR finding. Together these likely explain and close most of the current 0.93-point regression.
findings.risk: z-loss coefficient too high can cost a little PPL (1e-4 is standard). Softcap changes logit scale, which affects the WikiText byte-PPL benchmark — apply identically at eval (it's part of the model forward, so it is). QK-norm adds 2 small RMSNorms inside the looped block — negligible params/throughput.

findings.title: BLT-style hash n-gram byte embeddings — the single best-documented byte-level input trick
findings.detail: Byte Latent Transformer (arXiv 2412.09871) ablations: hash n-gram embeddings are 'very effective with very large improvements in bits-per-byte'; smaller n matters most and per-n-gram vocab (bucket count) is the most significant hyperparameter. Implementation in /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/model/transformer.py: at MythosMini.__init__ (line 306) add nn.Embedding tables for n in {2,3,4} with e.g. 2048-4096 buckets each; in forward (line 334) compute a rolling polynomial hash of the trailing n bytes per position (pure tensor ops: gather + mod, causal by construction) and add the looked-up vectors to self.embed(tokens), normalized by (1+#tables). Param cost at 3x2048x96 = ~590k (total ~1.64M). The leaderboard efficiency metric divides by log10(params): log10(1.64M)/log10(1.05M)=1.032, so this pays off if it buys >3.2% overall — BLT's BPB gains at byte level make that very plausible, and richer input features should also lift BLiMP (morphology is n-gram-shaped). Sweep bucket count {1024, 2048, 4096} on short runs; n=2,3 alone is the cheapest variant (~390k params, 2.2% penalty).
findings.expected_gain: Largest expected wiki byte-PPL improvement of any single architecture change here (BLT calls it their most impactful component); likely BLiMP gains too. Must clear the ~3% efficiency hurdle — high probability given BLT's 'very large' characterization.
findings.risk: Param growth is wasted if gains land under the log penalty — validate on a 200M-token run first. Hash gather adds minor input-layer cost (negligible vs attention). Interacts with STM/SLERP phases only trivially (new tensors merge like any other).

findings.title: Mixture-of-Softmaxes head to break the rank-96 softmax bottleneck (also targets late-training saturation)
findings.detail: arXiv 2404.07647 shows small LMs saturate late in training because hidden dim << rank of the target next-token distribution; the logit head here is rank-96 over 257 classes (transformer.py:355, tied head). The saturation signature — performance drop then plateau late in training — is suspiciously similar to what STM rounds are fighting. Fix from Yang et al. (arXiv 1711.03953): K-component Mixture of Softmaxes. Implementation: replace the line-355 head with K=3 projections (96x96) + a K-way gate (96xK); logits_k = (W_k x) @ embed.weight.T, probs = sum_k g_k softmax(logits_k); train with NLL on mixed probs. Cost ~28k params (+0.1% efficiency penalty — negligible) and 3x head FLOPs, trivial since vocab=257. Must adapt compute_loss in training/loop.py:49 to log-prob inputs (use log of mixture via logsumexp over components for numerical safety) and the benchmark PPL code in src/mythosmini/benchmarks to consume log-probs.
findings.expected_gain: Directly attacks byte-PPL and the documented small-model late-training degeneration; the original MoS paper showed solid PPL gains precisely when dim < effective rank. Uncertain magnitude at 257-vocab (bottleneck was demonstrated at 32k vocabs), but the parameter cost is nearly free.
findings.risk: Main uncertainty: 257-way byte distributions may have effective rank < 96, making this a no-op. Mixture head complicates the FP4 QAT path and the eval code paths (BLiMP/ARC scoring use logprobs — must route through the same mixture). Test on a short run.

findings.title: Mix in TinyStories-style constrained-vocabulary data — the only documented route to Gemma-class coherence at ~1M params
findings.detail: TinyStories (arXiv 2305.07759) is the existence proof for the user's ambition: <10M-param (even 1-block) models produce fluent, multi-paragraph, grammatical, consistent stories when the TARGET DISTRIBUTION is narrowed (3-4-year-old vocabulary), whereas 125M GPT-2 trained on open web can't write coherent sentences. fineweb-edu is simply too hard a target for 1.05M params — no optimizer fixes that. Action: (a) cheap version — pull roneneldan/TinyStories-v2 (GPT-4-generated, ~2.2GB, free) and add it to the data pipeline in /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/data/ as a second source; (b) ambitious version — generate a custom corpus on the 5090 with a local teacher (Gemma-3-4B-it or Qwen2.5-7B via vLLM, ~1-2 days for 1B bytes) using TinyStories' template trick (random word triplets + story features) plus simple-QA formats shaped like ARC items. Schedule it SmolLM2-style (arXiv 2502.02737): stable phase 60% fineweb-edu top-decile / 40% stories; decay (annealing) phase upweight the highest-quality mix (fineweb-edu score-5 + stories + QA) — SmolLM2 showed reserving the best data for the LR-decay phase maximizes its impact. Config touch points: FINEWEB_* constants and quality_percent in config.py, cache builder under data/.
findings.expected_gain: By far the biggest lever on perceived output coherence (the stated user goal). Benchmark impact: BLiMP should rise (near-perfect grammar is the headline TinyStories result); ARC may rise with QA-format synthetic data; WikiText byte-PPL is the risk axis — mitigated by keeping >=50% fineweb-edu and annealing on a mix.
findings.risk: Distribution shift could regress wiki PPL (1/3 of overall score) if the web-text share falls too low — sweep the mixture ratio {20%, 40%, 60%} on short runs. Synthetic generation adds wall-clock GPU time competing with training runs.

findings.title: Baby Llama-style same-vocab ensemble distillation: train 2 disposable 10-50M byte teachers, distill into the 1M student
findings.detail: Baby Llama (arXiv 2308.02019, BabyLM winner lineage) distilled an ensemble (GPT-2 705M + LLaMA 360M) into a 58M student that EXCEEDED both teachers on BLiMP-style evals in the low-data regime — distillation beats direct training when data is constrained. Crucially, cross-tokenizer distillation from real Gemma into a byte model is NOT the way: arXiv 2604.07466 (byte-level interface) and ULD (arXiv 2402.12030) both report large degradations and call BPE-to-byte transfer an open problem. Instead exploit that this codebase can train BIG byte-level teachers cheaply: at 1.19 Mtok/s, a 25M-param dim-384 variant of the same architecture trains on 2B tokens in well under a day on the 5090. Plan: train 2 teachers (e.g., dim 384 and dim 256, different seeds/loop counts), then a distillation pass for the 1M student — modify compute_loss in /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/training/loop.py to add alpha*KL(student_logits || mean_teacher_probs) with teachers under torch.inference_mode() (same 257-byte vocab, so logit alignment is trivial — no OT/ULD machinery). Teachers fit easily in 32GB beside the 1M student; cache teacher logits to disk (257 floats/byte is large — store top-32 logits + remainder bucket to keep it ~70GB/2B tokens, or run teachers inline at ~halved throughput).
findings.expected_gain: Literature consistently shows distilled-small > directly-trained-small, with the BabyLM result specifically on BLiMP (1/3 of the leaderboard score). This is the highest-ceiling quality lever after data, and it reuses the entire existing pipeline for teacher training.
findings.risk: Multi-day project (teacher runs + distill run + storage). Inline teacher forward cuts the prized 1.19 Mtok/s throughput roughly in half unless logits are precomputed. Hyperparameters (temperature, alpha) need a short sweep; bad settings can underperform plain CE.

findings.title: Tighten data filter to top ~2.5% and repeat 4 epochs — repetition up to 4x is free (Muennighoff)
findings.detail: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models (Muennighoff et al., OpenReview j5BuTrEj35; 400+ runs) found repeating data up to 4 epochs gives loss nearly identical to fresh data, with value extending to ~16 epochs. Current setup takes the top 10% of fineweb-edu sample-100BT (DEFAULT_QUALITY_PERCENT=10.0 in /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/config.py:17) to fill 2B tokens with single-pass fresh data. Better: take the top 2.5% (predominantly fineweb-edu score-5 documents, per FINEWEB_SCORE_DISTRIBUTION at config.py:19 score-5 is 12% of the filtered pool, so top-2.5%-of-corpus is achievable from score 5 + best of score 4) and cycle it 4x within the same 2B-token budget. Average sample quality strictly rises at provably negligible repetition cost. Implementation: quality_percent 10.0 -> 2.5 plus epoch-cycling support in the token cache loader (data/ + TOKEN_CACHE_DIR logic, config.py:40-44). Cite also: 4-epoch repetition pairs perfectly with the TinyStories/annealing finding (repeat the best mixture, not the marginal documents).
findings.expected_gain: Quality-filtering gains at zero data-quantity cost; fineweb-edu ablations show score-5-heavy training lifts ARC-style benchmarks specifically — ARC-Easy is 1/3 of the leaderboard score. Cheap to implement and test.
findings.risk: fineweb-edu int scores are coarse (3/4/5), so 'top 2.5%' needs a tie-break (classifier float scores are available in the dataset). One caution from arXiv 2510.06548: heavily repeated/overtrained bases become more sensitive to post-training modification — watch STM/SFT phases for amplified drift.

findings.title: Retune weight decay for the 2000-tokens-per-param regime (current 0.01 is almost certainly too small)
findings.detail: Power Lines (arXiv 2505.13738, NeurIPS 2025) shows the optimal AdamW timescale tau = B/(eta*lambda*D) follows a power law DECREASING in tokens-per-parameter D/N — i.e., the more overtrained the model, the LARGER the optimal weight decay. This model sits at D/N ~2000, two orders of magnitude beyond any normal recipe, while /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/config.py:84 has weight_decay=0.01 (a Chinchilla-era default). Also, optimal lambda scales linearly with batch size, and arXiv 2510.19093 argues weight decay is what actually makes LR transfer work across scales. Action: joint mini-sweep with the LR finding — wd in {0.05, 0.1, 0.3} x peak_lr in {6e-3, 1e-2, 2e-2} on 100-200M-token runs (9 cells, each ~3 minutes at 1.19 Mtok/s — the whole grid costs under an hour). Apply wd only to 2D matrices, not embeddings/norms/LoRA (standard practice; the current build_nadamw at training/optimizer.py:8 decays everything including the tied embedding, which also distorts the LM head — fix by introducing param groups regardless of the sweep outcome).
findings.expected_gain: EMA-timescale theory predicts under-decayed overtrained models carry stale early-training components in their weights; correcting wd at extreme TPP gave consistent loss improvements in the paper. The param-group fix (no wd on tied embedding) is a known free win for tiny tied-embedding models.
findings.risk: Pure hyperparameter change; only cost is sweep compute. Larger wd interacts with SLERP merging (weights shrink toward a smaller-norm basin) — re-run the merge tournament rather than assuming old t values.

findings.title: Multi-byte prediction auxiliary heads (n=4-8): byte-level is exactly where MTP shines — but unproven at 1M params
findings.detail: Gloeckle et al. (arXiv 2404.19737, ICML 2024) Section 3.3: for BYTE-level models, 8-byte prediction 'achieves astounding improvements' over next-byte — +67% problems solved on MBPP, +20% on HumanEval — because individual bytes carry so little information that next-byte CE is a weak training signal; MTP densifies supervision. Counter-signal: the same paper finds MTP doesn't help small (<1B) subword models, so the tiny-scale byte-level combination is genuinely untested. Implementation is cheap here because vocab=257: add n-1 auxiliary heads in transformer.py (each a 96x96 projection feeding the tied embedding head, ~9k params each; or independent 96x257 heads, ~25k each), average their CE losses with weight ~0.3 in compute_loss (training/loop.py:49), and DELETE the heads before benchmarking so leaderboard param count and eval path are unchanged (heads are train-time only — params don't count if stripped from the submitted checkpoint). Alternative with similar motivation: token-order prediction aux loss (TOP, arXiv 2508.19228) which beat MTP at 340M-1.8B scales and needs only one extra head.
findings.expected_gain: If the byte-level MTP effect holds at this scale, expect better sample efficiency and notably better generation coherence (MTP's gains concentrate on generative quality — the user's stated goal). Cost is a few % training throughput.
findings.risk: Highest-variance finding in this list: the small-model null result may dominate the byte-level positive result. Strictly a short-run A/B before committing. Aux heads also interact with the looped-block STM phase (extra params to merge or freeze).

findings.title: GPT-BERT-style hybrid causal+masked objective — the technique that won BabyLM 2024 outright, directly targets BLiMP
findings.detail: Findings of the 2nd BabyLM Challenge (arXiv 2412.05149): GPT-BERT, a hybrid autoregressive+masked-LM training scheme on one shared model, won BOTH the strict and strict-small tracks, with BLiMP among the headline metrics — and BLiMP is 1/3 of this leaderboard's overall score. The idea ports cleanly to this decoder: with probability p~0.15-0.3 per batch, replace the causal next-byte objective with a masked-prediction variant (mask random byte spans in the input, predict them at their positions with a shifted/prefix attention arrangement; GPT-BERT does this by switching between causal and bidirectional masks — with FlexAttention already in place at transformer.py:175-195, swapping block masks per batch is straightforward). Keep the same head and loss plumbing in training/loop.py. BabyLM-scale evidence (10-100M words, small models) is the closest published regime to this project of anything found. Secondary BabyLM findings worth stealing: curriculum learning generally UNDERPERFORMED at this scale (multiple negative results across 2023-2024 — do not invest in difficulty-ordered curricula), while data remixing/rewriting and distillation (see Baby Llama finding) were the reproducible winners.
findings.expected_gain: GPT-BERT's margin over pure-causal baselines at BabyLM scale was largest on BLiMP/grammaticality — plausibly worth several tenths on the blimp third of the overall score. Also a useful negative result: skip curriculum work, saving experiment budget.
findings.risk: Mask-mode batches reduce causal-LM training share, which could cost wiki byte-PPL; sweep the mixing ratio. The sparse-indexer/Flex short path needs a bidirectional mask variant — moderate plumbing in the Attention.forward paths (transformer.py:140-260). NaN-prone phases (STM) should keep pure-causal mode.

findings.title: Do NOT port nGPT wholesale; steal only its cheap pieces if anything (negative/guard finding)
findings.detail: nGPT (arXiv 2410.01131, NVIDIA, ICLR 2025) claims 4-20x token-efficiency by unit-normalizing every weight matrix and hidden state on the hypersphere — superficially attractive here (it would even make the SLERP tournament in reslerp.py geometrically natural, since weights live on spheres). However: (a) the speedup claims are measured at 0.5-1B params and 1k-8k context (4x at 1k ctx; this repo trains at 512, where the claimed gain is smallest); (b) independent replications through 2025 are mixed, with several groups reporting the advantage shrinks or vanishes after tuning the baseline; (c) it would require rewriting every module in /home/lane/MythosMini/src/mythosmini/model/transformer.py, conflicts with FP4 QAT (per-step weight renormalization fights the quantizer's scale calibration), with the per-loop LoRA deltas, and with the DSA sparse indexer scoring. The defensible subset: QK-norm (already in the stability finding) and embedding-norm housekeeping. Verdict from this research pass: file under 'revisit only if a major rearchitecture happens anyway'.
findings.expected_gain: Zero direct gain — this finding's value is preventing a multi-week refactor with poor expected value at 512-token context and FP4-QAT constraints, redirecting effort to Muon/data/distillation which have stronger evidence at this exact scale.
findings.risk: Small chance the nGPT gains are real and large even at 512 ctx for tiny models (the paper didn't test this regime); if all other levers are exhausted, a dim-96 nGPT prototype is a ~1-week experiment.
